pass_a_gloss: [Completing the previous section: who is the one] going to hear, or what will be the profit (ὄνησις) of the words? For no one will understand, except only God who knows all things; for in spirit, he says, he speaks mysteries. And observe how the one speaking to God speaks in spirit; God, then, after all, is the Spirit. Therefore the one speaking in a tongue speaks to God rather, he says, and not to men; but the one prophesying speaks to men building-up and exhortation and consolation (παραμυθία). Understanding, then, that prophesying in these [words] is interpreting the things of the prophets, through which the word of exhortation (παράκλησις) is made trustworthy (πιστόω) and the mind of those being initiated is led by the hand (χειραγωγέω) into the truth in Christ, he shows beforehand (προαποδείκνυμι) also in another way that interpreting the things of the prophets is incomparably among the better things than speaking in a tongue; for the one speaking in a tongue, he says, builds himself up; for he himself understands, but another wholly no one; but the one using for testimony the voices and foretellings (πρόρρησις) of the holy prophets builds up a church. Greater, then, after all, and among the highest boasts (αὔχημα) is prophesying, and among bright hopes, if indeed building up a church is admittedly better than conversing in a tongue with oneself and alone. [Lemma] I wish you all to speak in tongues, but rather that you prophesy, etc. Since it was a marvel and truly God-given (θεόσδοτος) that men being Hebrews could speak in the tongues of others, so that no one might suppose the apostle to determine (καθορίζω) without counsel (ἀβούλως) about what had happened, saying that what was granted through the working of the Spirit is worthless (εἰκαῖος), for it has been given for a sign to the believers, he accepts the thing and says, I wish all to speak in tongues. But he crops short (ἀποκείρω) at once clearly the zeal in this at least, and moves them over (μεθίστημι) toward the better, adding straightaway, but rather that you prophesy, saying most vividly that the one prophesying is greater than the one speaking in a tongue; and he shows that that [gift] is not wholly without benefit (ἀνόνητος) to those having it and to those hearing, adding, unless he interprets, that is, unless he has someone always sitting beside (προσεδρεύω) and interpreting for those being initiated. [Heading] Tome Five, Discourse Three. [Lemma] And none of them is voiceless (ἄφωνος). Some were coming into (εἰσφοιτάω) the churches who had been enriched by the working of the Spirit with being able to speak in tongues; then, it being needful to make the prayers in them, and before these the supplications (λιτή) or psalm-singings, using the tongue of those present, being able [to do so], this they did not do, but priding themselves (ἐναβρύνομαι) on the gift of tongues alone, they made neither prayers nor psalm-singing. This Paul teaches: that if those hearing are not knowers of the tongue in which the one having the gift should converse, no benefit is from the thing; for countless are the nations and many the tongues of men; and voiceless is none of those once counted among the rational or among men. He says that wholly none of those counted among the rational, or among men, is voiceless; but if someone perhaps should not know the force of each one's voice, and those again should not be knowers of his tongue, they will be barbarians to one another, although speaking correctly according to the own voice of each. It is needful, then, that those wishing to teach others should belch out (ἐρεύγομαι) the word familiar to the hearers; but if the sound (φθόγγος) were without sign (ἄσημος) and the voice unfamiliar, he has made in vain, only dashing (προσαράσσω) the hearing of the learner with a random crash (κτύπος). It is needful, he says, that those wishing to teach speak a word familiar to the hearers, since he toils in vain; for speaking in tongues alone does not build up a church. [Lemma] For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays. Spirit in these [words is] the [gift] through the [Spirit; continued in the next section].
pass_b_english: …to hear, or what profit will the words bring? For no one will understand except God alone, who knows all things. “For he speaks mysteries in the Spirit,” he says (1 Corinthians 14:2). Notice how the one who speaks to God speaks in the Spirit: so the Spirit is God. Therefore the one who speaks in a tongue, he says, speaks to God rather than to men; “but the one who prophesies speaks to men for building up, encouragement and consolation” (1 Corinthians 14:3).

Knowing, then, that “to prophesy” here means interpreting the writings of the prophets, through which the word of encouragement is made sure and the mind of those being instructed in the mysteries is led by the hand to the truth concerning Christ, he shows in another way as well that interpreting the prophets ranks incomparably higher than speaking in a tongue. “The one who speaks in a tongue,” he says, “builds up himself” (1 Corinthians 14:4), for he understands, but no one else at all does. But the one who uses the words and predictions of the holy prophets as testimony builds up the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). So prophesying is the greater thing and belongs among the highest grounds for boasting and among bright hopes, if indeed it is admittedly better to build up the church than to speak in a tongue to oneself alone.

“Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy,” and so on (1 Corinthians 14:5). It was something wonderful and truly God-given that men who were Hebrews could speak the languages of others. So that no one would think the apostle was rashly passing judgment on what had happened, by calling worthless what had been bestowed through the working of the Spirit (for it was given as a sign to believers), he welcomes the thing and says, “I want you all to speak in tongues.” But at once he plainly cuts short their eagerness for it and turns them to what is better, adding immediately, “but even more to prophesy,” and stating most clearly that the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in a tongue (1 Corinthians 14:5). Yet he shows that the gift is not altogether useless either to those who have it or to those who hear, when he adds, “unless he interprets” (1 Corinthians 14:5), that is, unless he has someone always at his side to interpret for those being instructed in the mysteries.

“And none of them is voiceless” (1 Corinthians 14:10). Some people used to come into the churches who had been enriched, by the working of the Spirit, with the ability to speak in tongues. Then, when they ought to have offered the prayers in the churches, and before these the litanies or the psalmody, using the language of those present, which they were able to do, they did not do it. Priding themselves only on the gift of tongues, they offered neither prayers nor psalmody. Paul teaches this: if the hearers do not know the language in which the one who has the gift is speaking, nothing is gained from it. For there are countless nations and many human languages, and none of those once counted among rational beings, or among men, is voiceless.

He says that none of those counted among rational beings, that is, among men, is altogether voiceless. But if someone does not know the meaning of another’s speech, and the others in turn do not know his language, they will be foreigners to one another (1 Corinthians 14:11), even though each speaks correctly in his own tongue. So those who wish to teach others must utter speech familiar to their hearers. But if the sound has no clear meaning and the speech is unfamiliar, he has labored in vain, merely striking the learner’s ear with an empty noise (1 Corinthians 14:9).
